https://www.budapesttimes.hu/hungary/mag.text: The Budapest Times Magyar’s message to the masses: ‘We are not Hungary’s Got Talent’ The Prime Minister announced on Sunday that he intends to introduce legislative amendments to shorten investigations and criminal proceedings related to the recovery of state assets. In a Facebook post, Péter Magyar wrote that no one wants the recovery of assets and the punishment of those responsible more than the government, but the rule-of-law framework must still be observed, as that is the only way the process can be credible. Responding to allegations concerning the National Asset Recovery and Asset Protection Authority, the Prime Minister stated that it is well known why it is in the interest of Fidesz and other fallen politicians to obstruct the authority’s work and undermine its credibility. He added that the government will not allow this discrediting campaign, as its goal is to establish the strongest possible authority, with professionally committed leaders who will never compromise. Péter Magyar also noted that “the right decision is not always the most popular one.” He elaborated that the members and representatives of the Tisza government had committed to four years of service and sworn an oath to their country, and that they subordinate everything to this and make every decision with that in mind, even when a given decision does not appear popular at the time. He wrote that anyone who distances themselves from Tisza over a personnel decision they dislike is free to make that choice, but the government will not yield — under any pressure — either on its oath or on its commitments. He stated that the government never committed to putting every leadership appointment to a public vote. In his view, it is not the responsibility of the public and citizens to determine who is the most suitable candidate for a given position — that responsibility lies with the person making the appointment. He added that if the public were always to decide on appointments, legislation, the budget, and taxes, the country would become ungovernable. He made clear that, as far as he is concerned, the matter is closed, and that they will continue governing “and building a functioning and humane Hungary.” The Prime Minister also assessed the first 110 days of the Tisza government in his post. Among other things, he reported on the unlocking of EU funds and the improvement of the budget’s position, citing as good news the 100,000-forint back-to-school support, the reduction of VAT on firewood and prescription medicines, the doubling of the social firewood allocation, and the planned increase of the minimum old-age pension to 120,000 forints in 2027. The Prime Minister stated that, in an act of solidarity not seen before, the country had managed to weather three heatwaves and two energy crises.
